new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls on the first syllable of the phonological word; contrastive vowel length is likewise confined to the initial syllable. Verb roots are relatively unstressed and are analysed as belonging to the same phonological word as whatever precedes them, so they do not take their own initial stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said by Black 1980. Goedemans 1998 (App. D, Kurtjar T180) files it second-hand as 'main stress on the initial syllable, secondary stress on alternates', citing Black's 1977 manuscript dictionary.
new_statements.exceptions: Verb roots are 'relatively unstressed' and lack length contrasts; Black flags that treating them as part of the preceding word 'could prove simplistic'. No lexical exceptions. The sister language Kuthant differs: stress on the first long vowel, otherwise the first vowel (p.197).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the word as Black phonologises it (verb root plus preceding material forming one word). The statement is the fieldworker's own synchronic analysis ('here taken to'), embedded in a historical-comparative paper and based exclusively on his fieldwork from 1974 (p.187). Kurtjar is an initial-dropping language with initial clusters, so 'first syllable' means the synchronic post-loss word.
new_statements.identity_note: kung1262 'Kunggara' is a Glottolog Bookkeeping entry: ISO 639-3 CR 2015-004 retired [kvs] as a duplicate of Gurdjar [gdj] (adopted 2016-01-15). The description of record is therefore Kurtjar = Gurdjar, glottocode gurd1238 (Norman Pama, Pama-Nyungan; Normanton area, Gulf of Carpentaria). Black 1980 p.187 states explicitly that the Kurtjar 'acknowledge an alternative name kungkar' and that their data 'was more commonly elicited under the latter name - e.g. as Kunggara - by earlier investigators' (Tindale, Hale, Oates, Healey, Keen, Sommer, Breen, Sutton). the two keys should be merged into one catalog entry rather than counted twice.

sources.locator: Section 4 'Phonologies of the attested languages', Kurtjar, p.196 (p.16); length statement pp.195-196; identity ('Kunggara') p.187; Kuthant contrast p.197
sources.note: Sec. 4 'Phonologies of the attested languages', Kurtjar, p.196 (read on the page scan): stress falls predictably on the first syllable of the word; verb roots are relatively unstressed and are treated as part of the preceding phonological word; vowel length only in initial syllables (pp.195-196). p.197: sister language Kuthant has non-contrastive stress on the first long vowel, else the first vowel. p.187: Kurtjar self-name kurtYar, alternative name kungkar, data 'more commonly elicited under the latter name - e.g. as Kunggara'; based exclusively on Black's fieldwork from 1974.
